abstract: Objective This study aims to explore potential mechanisms associated with differentially abundant proteins and metabolites in rabbit plaques through integrated proteomics and untargeted metabolomics analyses. Methods Experimental rabbits were randomly divided into the model group and the sham group. Abdominal aortas were isolated, collected, and treated with proteinase K. Subsequently, a tandem mass tag (TMT)-labeled quantitative proteomics analysis and an untargeted metabolomics analysis via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) of abdominal aortas were performed to evaluate the possible protein and metabolite fingerprints in arterial plaques. Acquired data were analyzed using uni‐ and multivariate statistics. The correlation between differentially abundant proteins and metabolites was analyzed using the Pearson correlation coefficient strategy, and their possibly involved functional pathways were predicted by Kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis. Results Advanced plaques develop in the model group. A total of 207 proteins are significantly altered in injured aortas compared to uninjured ones, with 133 upregulated and 74 downregulated proteins (fold changes > 1.2, P < 0.05). In plaques, 234 metabolites are significantly changed under the positive ion mode, and 187 under the negative ion mode. Notably, increases are observed in phosphatidylcholines (PCs) [PC 9:0] and lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) [LPC 20:2], two key lipid components. These metabolites are involved in some key metabolic pathways, including purine metabolism and vascular smooth muscle contraction. Conclusions The results confirm the potential of integrated proteomics and untargeted metabolomics in exploring the molecular characteristics of atherosclerosis. Identified proteins and metabolites may serve as promising biomarkers for plaque diagnosis.

2
Materials and methods
2.1
Animal ethics
The experimental procedures involving rabbits were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Capital Medical University (AEEI-2022–283). All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations of Capital Medical University.
2.2
Rabbit atherosclerosis model establishment
Adult New Zealand white male rabbits (∼3.0 kg) were housed individually for 12 weeks at the Beijing Regal Experimental Animal Breeding Center (Beijing, China). They had access to light, ventilation, and
ad libitum
food and water. The rabbits were randomly assigned to either the sham group (n = 6) or the atherosclerosis group (n = 6). As described in our previous publication [
19
], abdominal aortas of rabbits in the atherosclerosis group were injured using balloons during the third week of the high-fat diet (HFD) period. At the end of the 12-week HFD period, all rabbits were euthanized with an intravenous pentobarbital preparation (100 mg/kg), and their abdominal aortas were isolated and prepared into equal-length segments. One segment was embedded in paraffin, sectioned, and stained. Other segments were stored at −80 °C for multi-omics and other analyses.
2.3
Ultrasound of plaques in abdominal aortas
Abdominal aorta ultrasound imaging was performed using a linear 4–14 MHz transducer with a Nuewa R9 ultrasound scanner (Shenzhen, China). The imaging setup and data acquisition procedures were established as described [
20
]. Each rabbit underwent routine CUS (carotid ultrasound) scanning of the abdominal aorta in the supine position with the head tilted contralaterally. B-mode digital video sequences of plaques were recorded by sweeping through the plaques in longitudinal, circumferential, and transverse directions, with and without color duplex (frame rates between 28 and 42 Hz). Images were acquired, and the intima-media thickness (IMT) of the abdominal aorta was measured and compared.
2.4
Histological staining of plaques
Serial paraffin sections, 5 μm thick, were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Masson's trichrome. Images of the stained sections were captured using a Pannoramic SCAN II scanner (Budapest, Hungary), and positive signals were quantified using ImageJ software. The plaque area and total luminal area of vessels were measured, and the index was expressed as the plaque area relative to the total artery area (%) using the formula.
2.5
Sample preparation for multi-omics analysis
For proteomics analysis, each sample was ground in liquid nitrogen and lysed using dissolved buffer (DB buffer) including 6 M urea and 100 mM TEAB, pH = 8.5. After 5 min of ultrasonication, the lysate was centrifuged at 12,000 g for 15 min at 4 °C. The resulting supernatant was treated with 10 mM DTT at 56 °C for 1 h to reduce disulfide bonds, followed by alkylation with iodoacetamide (IAM) for 1 h at room temperature (RT) in the dark. The samples were then subjected to precipitation by adding 4-fold precooled acetone and incubating at −20 °C for 2 h. After centrifugation at 12,000 g for 15 min at 4 °C, the resulting precipitate was washed with 1 mL of cold acetone and dissolved in dissolution buffer containing 8 M urea and 100 mM TEAB. For metabolomics analysis, 100 mg of tissue was ground in liquid nitrogen and homogenized in precooled 80 % methanol. After incubation on ice for 5 min, the homogenate was centrifuged at 15,000 g, 4 °C for 20 min. A portion of the resulting supernatant was diluted with LC-MS grade water to a final solution containing 53 % methanol.
2.6
Proteomics
Each protein specimen from the aorta was reconstituted using dissolution buffer containing 8 M urea and 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB). Trypsin and 100 mM TEAB buffer were added to the samples, and digestion was carried out at 37 °C for 4 h. Subsequently, trypsin and CaCl
2
were added, and overnight digestion was performed. Digested samples were acidified with formic acid (pH < 3) and centrifuged at 12,000 g for 5 min at RT. The supernatant was loaded onto a C18 desalting column, washed three times with washing buffer containing 0.1 % formic acid and 3 % acetonitrile, and eluted with elution buffer. Each eluent was collected and lyophilized. The dried samples were reconstituted in 100 μL of 0.1 M TEAB buffer, followed by addition of 41 μL of acetonitrile-dissolved tandem mass tag (TMT)-labelled reagent. After incubating for 2 h at RT, the reaction was quenched with 8 % ammonia. The labeled samples were combined in equal volumes, desalted, and lyophilized.
Fractionation was performed using a C18 column (BEH C18, Waters) on a Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The eluates were monitored at UV 214 nm, collected for a tube per minute and combined into 10 fractions finally. All fractions were dried under vacuum, and then, reconstituted in 0.1 % (v/v) formic acid (FA) in water. Subsequently, spectra from each run were analyzed against the 1854900-Oryctolagus_cuniculus.fasta (65088 sequences) database using the Proteome Discoverer 2.5 (PD 2.5, Thermo Fisher) search engine. Proteins with a fold change (FC) ≥ 1.2 and
P
< 0.05 were considered differentially expressed (DEPs).
2.7
Untargeted metabolomics
Frozen aortas were transferred to fresh tubes and centrifuged at 15,000g, 4 °C for 20 min. The resulting supernatant was injected into a UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher, Germany) coupled with an Orbitrap Q ExactiveTMHF mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher, Germany) [
21
]. Eluent A consisted of 0.1 % formic acid (FA) in water, and eluent B was methanol under positive polarity mode. Under negative polarity mode, eluent A was composed of 5 mM ammonium acetate, and eluent B was methanol. The gradient profile was programmed as follows: starting at 2 % B for 1.5 min, increasing from 2 % to 85 % B over 3 min, reaching 100 % B over 10 min, decreasing from 100 % to 2 % B over 10.1 min, and holding at 2 % B for 12 min. The Q ExactiveTMHF mass spectrometer operated in positive/negative polarity mode with a spray voltage of 3.5 KV, a capillary temperature of 320 °C, a sheath gas flow rate of 35 psi, an auxiliary gas flow rate of 10 L/min, an S-lens RF level of 60, and an auxiliary gas heater temperature of 350 °C.
The data files generated by UHPLC-MS/MS were processed by XCMS to perform peak alignment, peak picking, and quantitation for each metabolite. Then, based on adduct ions and setting mass deviation to 10 ppm, a comparison was made between these data and the self-built high-quality secondary spectrum database (NovoMetDB) to obtain results for metabolite identification. After eliminating background ions according to blank samples, the original quantitative results were normalized by the following formula to obtain relative peak areas: Relative peak areas = Raw quantitative value of samples/(The sum of quantitative value of samples/The sum of quantitative value of QC1). Compounds with a coefficient of variation (CV) of relative peak areas in QC samples greater than 30 % were removed. Finally, the identification and relative quantitation results of metabolites were obtained. Data processing is based on the Linux operating system (CentOS version 6.6), using R (R-3.4.3, R-4.0.3) and Python (Python-2.7.6, Python-3.5.0). The search engine used for the feature detection is Compound Discoverer 3.3, and the database used for feature identification are mzCloud, mzVault and MassList. The metabolites identified by untargeted metabolomics are annotated according to the IDC level of the Metabolomics Standards Initiative. The level of metabolites annotated by mzcloud and mzvault is the level 2, and the level of metabolites annotated by masslist is the level 3.
2.8
Correlation analysis of proteomics and metabolomics
Differentially expressed proteins and metabolites were mapped to the KEGG pathway database to identify shared pathways, encompassing both biochemical and signal transduction pathways. The top ten differentially expressed proteins and the top five abundant metabolites were selected for interaction analysis. This involved creating network diagrams to visually illustrate potential correlations between metabolites and proteins.
2.9
Statistical analysis
Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Paired group comparisons were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, while unpaired group comparisons were conducted using the Mann-Whitney test.
Pearson
correlation coefficient was utilized for correlation analysis, with R
2
> 0.8 indicating a strong correlation between groups. Statistical significance between groups was defined as
P
< 0.05. Raw data from proteomics and metabolomics were analyzed using statistical software including R (version 3.4.3), Python (version 2.7.6), and CentOS (release 6.6) [
22
]. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software version 9.4.0 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA).

1
Introduction
Atherosclerosis is a major pathological basis of most cardiovascular diseases, characterized by excessive inflammation and lipid metabolism dysfunction [
1
,
2
]. This disease imposes serious social and economic burdens, making the investigation of its mechanisms for effective intervention a hot topic in cardiovascular research [
3
]. However, specific molecular signatures of atherosclerosis are poorly understood, limiting its precise diagnosis and effective treatment. Advanced omics approaches, such as transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, etc., which have wide biological applications, are now utilized for understating the complex characteristics associated with atherosclerosis [
[4]
,
[5]
,
[6]
]. Recently, integrative multi-omics strategies have been employed to uncover deeper features of arterial plaques, identifying potential candidates in atherosclerosis pathogenesis, such as long non-coding RNAs and other inflammatory factors [
7
,
8
].
Cardiovascular transcriptomics is now used to reveal cell subtype-specific gene expression patterns in atherosclerotic aortas of various animal models through differential gene expression analysis [
9
]. Microarray and bulk RNA sequencing (RNAseq) are the most common methods for transcriptomic evaluation. Notably, single-cell RNAseq enables the determination of transcriptomes at the cellular level [
4
]. Cardiovascular proteomics, which facilitate protein separation, identification, and characterization, enhance our understanding of cardiovascular features at the protein level by analyzing complex biological mixtures. This aids in discovering new strategies for preventing, identifying, and treating cardiovascular diseases [
10
,
11
]. As an emerging omics method, untargeted metabolomics characterizes the metabolic landscape of arterial plaques. These metabolites, being the end products of genetic and environmental influences, offer a functional link between genotype and phenotype, deepening our understanding of atherosclerosis and informing its management [
12
,
13
]. Integrative multi-omics strategies can provide more comprehensive information by combining two or three omics methods, depending on the study purpose, as applied in many current studies on atherosclerosis [
14
,
15
].
Combining proteomics with metabolomics is an integrative research approach to uncover interactions between proteins and metabolites in living organisms [
16
,
17
]. Proteomics studies the types, structures, functions, and changes in biological processes of proteins, while metabolomics investigates the types, contents, and transformation patterns of metabolites, such as small organic molecules. Metabolites and proteins are intricately linked: as substrates and enzymes, in allosteric interactions, and in the assembly of protein complexes [
18
]. Thus, integrating proteomics and metabolomics provides a comprehensive understanding of biological processes and reveals key regulatory mechanisms involved in atherosclerosis. We combined quantitative proteomics analysis using tandem mass tags (TMTs) with untargeted metabolomics analysis via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to identify potent molecular signatures of atherosclerotic plaques in rabbits, and gain insights into the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis.

3
Results
3.1
Advanced plaques develop in the injured abdominal aortas
The rabbit abdominal atherosclerosis model is successfully established using the HFD plus balloon injury strategy. Ultrasound imaging reveals that the intima-media thickness (IMT) of lesions in the injured abdominal aorta (0.75 ± 0.36 mm) is significantly greater than that in the uninjured abdominal aorta (0.33 ± 0.03 mm,
P
< 0.05), depicted in
Fig. 1A
. In a similar vein, pathological staining of sequential aorta sections illustrates increased plaque formation in the model group (
Fig. 1
,
Fig. 1
), validating larger plaque development in the injured abdominal aorta compared to the uninjured aorta. HE staining and quantitative analysis reveals that the ratio of plaque area to total artery area is 13.16 ± 10.18 for the uninjured abdominal aorta and 42.98 ± 16.10 for the injured abdominal aorta, with a significant difference observed (
P
< 0.05) (
Fig. 1B
). Additionally, Masson's trichrome staining exhibits a similar pattern, as shown in
Fig. 1C
. These findings collectively validate the progression of plaque development in atherosclerotic rabbits and affirm the suitability of the specimens for subsequent multi-omics analyses.
Fig. 1
Rabbit atherosclerosis model is successfully established. Male New Zealand white rabbits were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) and randomly divided into the atherosclerosis group and the sham group. The atherosclerosis group was injured with a balloon in their abdominal aortas, and the sham group had a skin incision only. Ultrasound and pathological analysis, including H&E and Masson staining, were performed to show the formation of plaques. A. Ultrasound results of abdominal aortas. B. H&E staining of arterial lesions in abdominal aortas. C. Masson staining of arterial lesions in abdominal aortas.
3.2
Differentially expressed proteins are identified in arterial plaques
A tandem mass tag (TMT)-labeled quantitative proteomic analysis is conducted to compare protein expression profiles between the two groups. The relative abundance of differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) is assessed accordingly. The volcano plot provides an overview of all detected proteins in plaques from the rabbit atherosclerosis model. In this representation, black dots denote proteins with no significant differential expression, red dots indicate upregulated proteins, and green dots represent downregulated proteins. Our study identifies 207 proteins with significantly different expression levels between the model group and the control group. Specifically, 74 proteins are notably upregulated, while 133 proteins are markedly downregulated (
Fig. 2A
). Hierarchical clustering analysis is then performed on the relative abundance of DEPs in each sample, revealing distinct protein expression patterns between the sham group and the atherosclerosis group (
Fig. 2B
). In summary, clustering proteins based on their expression patterns effectively visualize differences in protein profiles between the two groups.
Fig. 2
Identification of differentially expressed proteins in arterial plaques. A. Volcano plot of differentially expressed proteins in arterial plaques. B. Hierarchical clustering analysis of differentially expressed proteins in arterial plaques.
3.3
Functional enrichment analyses of differentially expressed proteins in arterial plaques reveal possibly involved pathways in atherosclerosis
A total of 207 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in arterial plaques are identified and subjected to Gene Ontology (GO) term and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses to elucidate their biological roles. GO analysis categorizes the 207 proteins into three main categories: biological process (BP), cellular component (CC), and molecular function (MF). Specifically, the primary terms identified are cellular aromatic compound metabolism and heterocycle metabolic process for BP, cell periphery for CC, and carboxy-lyase activity for MF (
Fig. 3A
). Furthermore, enrichment analysis reveals their involvement in various pathways, including carbon metabolism, biosynthesis of amino acids, RNA degradation, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling pathway, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and dilated cardiomyopathy (
Fig. 3B
). These findings collectively suggest potential biological functions of the identified DEPs in arterial plaques.
Fig. 3
Functional analyses of differentially expressed proteins in arterial plaques. A. Go terms of differentially expressed proteins in arterial plaques. B. KEGG pathways of differentially expressed proteins in arterial plaques.
3.4
Differentially abundant metabolites are detected in arterial plaques
In addition to proteomics, metabolomics is conducted using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) in both negative and positive ion modes, enabling comprehensive detection of metabolites in arterial plaques. In the negative ion mode, 187 metabolites exhibit significantly different expression patterns in atherosclerotic rabbits, with 110 metabolites upregulated and 77 metabolites downregulated (
Fig. 4A
). Conversely, the analysis in the positive ion mode reveals 234 metabolites with markedly different expression patterns in the model group, including 141 upregulated and 93 downregulated metabolites (
Fig. 4B
). Therefore, comparisons of differential metabolites between the two groups are depicted.
Fig. 4
Identification of differentially expressed metabolites in arterial plaques. A. Volcano plot of differentially expressed metabolites under the negative ion mode. B. Volcano plot of differentially expressed metabolites under the positive ion mode. C. Matchstick diagram of differentially expressed metabolites under the negative ion mode. D. Matchstick diagram of differentially expressed metabolites under the positive ion mode.
Additionally, matchstick diagrams list the top ten differentially abundant metabolites in both negative and positive ion modes (
Fig. 4C, D
). In the negative ion mode, metabolites such as LPG 20:2, LPG 18:1, LPG 17:1, LPE 22:1, LPC O-20:1, LPI 20:2, LPI 18:3, LPS 16:0, LPG 17:0, and PC O-16:1_2:0 are upregulated in atherosclerotic rabbits, whereas (2S)-4-Oxo-2-phenyl-3,4-dihydro-2H-chromen-7-yl-beta-D-glucopyranoside, 2,3-Dinor-TXB2, oxoadipic acid, N-acetylaspartic acid, and PC 17:0_20:4 are downregulated. In the positive ion mode, metabolites such as PC 9:0, quinolinic acid, DPH, CAR 16:1, lysopg 18:1, tyrosylalanine, CAR 17:1, CAR 22:2, LPE 18:3, and CAR 18:2 are upregulated, whereas 5-methoxyindole-3-carbaldehyde, L-ergothioneine, hydroquinone, N-acetyl-DL-phenylalanine, and methyl 3-indolyacetate are downregulated. These findings highlight promising metabolite candidates associated with atherosclerosis.
3.5
Correlation analyses of differentially abundant metabolites demonstrate metabolite change consistency/inconsistency in arterial plaques
To assess synergistic or antagonistic relationships among differentially abundant metabolites, correlation analyses are conducted using the
Pearson
correlation coefficient. Heatmaps depict these relationships among metabolite pairs (
Fig. 5A and B
). In the negative ion mode, 3-phosphoglyceric acid exhibits positive correlations with phosphoenolpyruvic acid, L-tyrosinemethylester, cAMP, and adenosine-5′-diphosphoglucose, and negative correlations with LPI 16:0, LPC 16:2, LPC 22:1, LPA 18:0, and LPS 18:0 (
Fig. 5A
). Moreover, LPI 16:0 shows positive correlations with LPE 22:1, LPC 16:2, LPC 22:1, LPA 18:0, and LPS 18:0, and negative correlations with phosphoenolpyruvic acid, P-toluenesulfonic acid, MAM2201 N-pentanoic acid metabolite, L-tyrosinemethylester, cAMP, and adenosine-5′-diphosphoglucose (
Fig. 5A
). In the positive ion mode, phosphopyruvic acid shows positive correlations with DLK, SPB 16:1;2O, AL 8810 methyl ester, riboflavin, DL-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, and 3-phospho-D-glyceric acid, and negative correlations with LPC 18:1-SN1, cholesterol, thiazolidine-4-carboxylic acid, and LPC 24:2-SN1. Furthermore, cholesterol exhibits positive correlations with thiazolidine-4-carboxylic acid and LPC 24:2-SN1, and negative correlations with DLK, 5-methoxyindole-3-carbaldehyde, DL-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, and 3-phospho-D-glyceric acid (
Fig. 5B
).
Fig. 5
Correlation analysis of differentially expressed metabolites in arterial plaques. A. Correlation map under the negative mode. B. Correlation map under the positive mode. C, D. The chord diagram shows molecular pairs of metabolites with correlation coefficient |r|>0.8 and p < 0.05, which can more intuitively reveal the co-regulatory relationship between various metabolites. C. The chord diagram under the negative mode. D. The chord diagram under the positive mode.
The top 20 differentially abundant metabolites are selected to illustrate the correlations between various metabolite categories using chord diagrams (
Fig. 5C, D
). In the negative ion mode, lipids and related molecular metabolites are positively correlated. In the positive ion mode, lipids and related molecular metabolites are positively correlated with nucleotides, nucleotide analogs, and organic oxygen compounds (
Fig. 5C, D
). These findings suggest the potential importance of lipids and lipid-like molecules in plaque formation.
3.6
KEGG analysis of differentially abundant metabolites reveals the possible functional pathways involved in arterial plaque formation
To further investigate the functional pathways involving these differentially abundant metabolites, KEGG analysis is employed. Then, some enriched pathways are identified in the context of atherosclerosis, including primary biochemical metabolic and signal transduction pathways. In the negative ion mode, the top 20 enriched pathways for these metabolites are pyruvate metabolism, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, vascular smooth muscle contraction, riboflavin metabolism, propanoate metabolism, phosphonate and phosphinate metabolism, phospholipase D signaling pathway, oocyte meiosis, necroptosis, MAPK signaling pathway, longevity regulating pathway, linoleic acid metabolism, hedgehog signaling pathway, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, fructose and mannose metabolism, folate biosynthesis, endocrine resistance, chemokine signaling pathway, and adrenergic signaling in cardiomyocytes (
Fig. 6A
). In the positive ion mode, the top 20 enriched pathways include steroid hormone biosynthesis, vitamin digestion and absorption, tryptophan metabolism, nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism, galactose metabolism, steroid biosynthesis, prolactin signaling pathway, synaptic vesicle cycle, primary bile acid biosynthesis, platelet activation, phosphatidylinositol signaling system, long-term depression, inositol phosphate metabolism, gap junction, Fc epsilon Rl signaling pathway, estrogen signaling pathway, endocrine resistance, drug metabolism-cytochrome P450, circadian entrainment, and biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids (
Fig. 6B
). These findings predict several functional pathways potentially involved in atherosclerosis, which may attract special attention from researchers in the future.
Fig. 6
Functional analyses of differentially expressed metabolites in arterial plaques. A: KEGG enrichment analysis under the negative mode: pyruvate metabolism, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and vascular smooth muscle contraction. B: KEGG enrichment analysis under the positive mode: steroid hormone biosynthesis, vitamin digestion and absorption, tryptophan metabolism, nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism, galactose metabolism, steroid biosynthesis, and prolactin signaling pathway.
3.7
Correlation analysis of differentially expressed proteins and metabolites shows the metabolite and protein associations under positive and negative ion models
The top ten differentially expressed proteins and the top five differentially abundant metabolites are selected to investigate potential associations between these proteins and metabolites. In the negative ion mode, LPI 18:3 is positively co-expressed with

KEGG analysis demonstrates some pathways in which these differentially abundant metabolites and differentially expressed proteins are together enriched
Using differentially abundant metabolites and differentially expressed proteins as targets, KEGG analysis is performed again to predict functional pathways with reduced background interference. In the negative ion mode, the most enriched pathways include metabolism-related pathways, vascular smooth muscle contraction, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, fructose and mannose metabolism, pyrimidine metabolism, purine metabolism, carbon metabolism, and tyrosine metabolism (
Fig. 8A
). In the positive ion mode, the most enriched pathways are galactose metabolism, tryptophan metabolism, phosphatidylinositol signaling system, vascular smooth muscle contraction, purine metabolism, and tyrosine metabolism (
Fig. 8B
). Notably, some pathways overlap in both modes, such as vascular smooth muscle contraction, purine metabolism, and tyrosine metabolism, which may play a crucial role in atherosclerosis progression.

4
Discussion
Proteins and metabolites are closely linked through enzymatic or transport reactions, playing key roles in many biological functions [
23
,
24
]. However, few studies have simultaneously evaluated the proteome and metabolome during atherosclerosis progression. To this end, an integrated proteomics and metabolomics approach has been used to identify differentially expressed proteins and metabolites in plaques and meanwhile investigate their functional pathways [
[25]
,
[26]
,
[27]
]. In this study, integrated quantitative proteomics using tandem mass tags (TMTs) combined with untargeted metabolomics using non-targeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) on rabbit atherosclerotic aortas is employed to reveal molecular signatures of atherosclerotic plaques. This approach not only identifies differentially expressed proteins and metabolites but also uncovers associations between them, thereby providing valuable insights into the metabolic and proteomic alterations associated with atherosclerosis.
An interesting finding from this study's proteomics analysis is that differentially expressed proteins in arterial plaques are mostly enriched in several well-known metabolic pathways, including galactose metabolism, carbon metabolism, biosynthesis of amino acids, and the AMPK signaling pathway. AMPK, as a master switch for energy, is responsible for the balance of lipogenesis and lipolysis, and determines energy homeostasis [
28
,
29
]. Current studies report that the AMPK signaling pathway is highly involved in the initiation and progression of atherosclerosis [
30
,
31
]. Some atypical chemokines, such as macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) and d-dopachrome tautomerase (D-DT), participate in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis by modulating the AMPK pathway [
32
,
33
]. Notably, MIF-2 exerts a pro-atherogenic role and promotes hepatic lipid accumulation through AMPK- and AKT-SREBP-mediated signaling pathways and CXCR4/CD74 receptor complexes [
33
,
34
]. Additionally, galactose metabolism contributes to plaque formation. Galectin-3 (Gal-3), a 30 kDa β-galactose-binding protein, has been identified as a novel inflammatory factor for atherosclerosis, participating in intravascular inflammation, lipid endocytosis, monocyte chemotaxis, macrophage activation, cellular proliferation, and cell adhesion [
35
,
36
]. Thus, these metabolic pathways, enriched with differentially expressed proteins, play important roles in atherosclerosis. Other less-studied pathways may also provide new candidates for mechanistic exploration in the process of plaque progression.
In this regard, untargeted metabolomics data from our study revealed that differentially abundant metabolites are predominantly enriched in pyruvate metabolism, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and vascular smooth muscle contraction under the negative ion mode. In the positive ion mode, they are mainly enriched in steroid hormone biosynthesis, vitamin digestion and absorption, tryptophan metabolism, nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism, galactose metabolism, steroid biosynthesis, and the prolactin signaling pathway. These findings align, at least partially, with current publications by other researchers [
[37]
,
[38]
,
[39]
]. Additionally, we analyze functional pathways in which both differentially expressed proteins and metabolites are enriched, and identify overlapping pathways in both ion modes, such as vascular smooth muscle contraction, purine metabolism, and tyrosine metabolism. Consistent with our results, Li and colleagues have found that significantly downregulated genes are enriched in vascular smooth muscle contraction and the cGMP-PKG signaling pathway [
40
], while Kang
et al.
have showed that differentially expressed genes are substantially enriched in glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, tyrosine metabolism, tryptophan metabolism, β-alanine metabolism, fatty acid biosynthesis, and starch and sucrose metabolism [
41
]. To date, more metabolomics studies combined with other omics methods are being integrated to identify specific differentially expressed genes, proteins, and metabolites, providing more reliable evidence to understand the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.
Furthermore, phosphatidylcholines (PCs) [PC 9:0] and lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) [LPC 20:2], two key lipid components, have been observed to increase in atherosclerotic rabbits compared to controls. PCs generally serve as the major dietary source of choline [
42
], and LPCs, derived from the cleavage of PCs, are main components of oxidized low-density lipoproteins contributing to atherosclerosis [
43
]. PCs are the most abundant phospholipids in mammalian cell membranes, playing a crucial role in regulating lipid, lipoprotein, and whole-body energy metabolism, as demonstrated in numerous in vivo studies [
44
,
45
]. Cole and coworkers have revealed that impaired biosynthesis of PCs attenuates plaque formation and prevents lipotoxic cardiac dysfunction in
Apoe
-/-
mice [
46
]. Although elevated LPC levels are associated with atherosclerosis complications, it is still debated whether LPCs exert a pro- or anti-atherogenic role [
47
,
48
]. Therefore, the role of LPCs in atherosclerosis remains under investigation. Nevertheless, our data provide useful indications for further exploration of the metabolic mechanisms of atherosclerosis associated with PCs and LPCs.
It has been revealed that complex interactions among proteins, lipid metabolites and the gut microbiota jointly affect atherosclerosis [
[49]
,
[50]
,
[51]
]. Zhao and colleagues have observed that GRb1 regulates phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) metabolic dysregulation by reducing the relative abundance of Helicobacter_typhlonius in an atherosclerosis co-depression comorbidity model, suggesting a strong correlation among Helicobacter_typhlonius, phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and CD44 in atherosclerotic progression [
49
]. Yu
et al.
have screened 6 kinds of differentially expressed proteins with the highest correlation to differential metabolites for predicting the onset of early atherosclerosis, and meanwhile performed qPCR to validate them [
50
]. In this study, we have also revealed some metabolite and protein associations under positive and negative ion models, suggesting potential molecular mechanisms of atherosclerosis. However, detailed regulatory mechanisms still need more experimental exploration. Interestingly, PC O-16:1_2:0 is found to be upregulated in atherosclerotic rabbits, whereas PC 17:0_20:4 is shown to be downregulated. The increase in PC O-16:1_2:0 is closely related to the inflammatory process of atherosclerosis [
52
], and the reduction in PC 17:0_20:4 reflects the disruption of cell membrane integrity and the loss of anti-inflammatory precursors in atherosclerotic plaques [
53
]. This explanation is in line with our finding.
Although the integrated proteomics and metabolomics analysis of plaques provides many meaningful protein and metabolite insights, we acknowledge several limitations in this study. Firstly, we have not verified the expression of these differentially abundant proteins and metabolites through other methods such as RT-PCR and Western blot, which should be done in the next step. Targeted metabolomics is planned to be perform by using a separate cohort. Nevertheless, similar findings from other studies could enhance the credibility of our results. Secondly, the specific correlations between proteins and corresponding metabolites should be investigated
in vitro
using cell lines and
in vivo
using atherosclerosis animal models through knockin and/or knockout techniques. This would provide a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying this disease. At last, the technical limitation of untargeted metabolomics can lead to the inaccuracy of identified metabolites. Several exogenous metabolites that are not supposed to present in plaques whereas annotated in this study, may draw some concerns. In our context, more attention should be paid to endogenous metabolites.
In brief, identifying a panel of differentially expressed proteins and metabolites as biomarkers for detecting atherosclerotic plaque progression is a significant achievement in precision medicine. This advancement has the potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and facilitate tailored therapeutic approaches. Integrating these biomarkers into clinical practice promises early diagnosis, intervention, and targeted treatments, thereby optimizing patient outcomes and potentially reducing the disease burden. Combining proteomics and metabolomics with other omics methods further enhances our understanding of atherosclerosis mechanisms.
5
Conclusions
In summary, this study presents an integrated analysis of metabolomics and proteomics data from the abdominal aortas of atherosclerotic rabbits and controls. The identified characteristic proteins and metabolites form a complex network, illustrating the critical functional pathways associated with atherosclerosis. Key metabolic pathways, such as vascular smooth muscle contraction, purine metabolism, and tyrosine metabolism, were highlighted as crucial mechanisms involving protein-metabolite associations in plaque progression. These altered proteins and metabolites, serving as promising molecular targets, may offer valuable diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for atherosclerosis. Future studies should explore the functional co-regulation of proteins and metabolites and apply these promising candidates.
